title: Karmic tail 12-16-4 in the destiny matrix: an emperor upside down, lightning and a throne

seo.title: Karmic tail 12-16-4 “The Emperor” in the destiny matrix
seo.description: 12-16-4 is called “The Emperor”. Why the Hanged Man is the Emperor upside down, where tyranny hides in the cards and how to leave the endure-and-collapse loop.

short: 12-16-4 is the karmic tail that popular Russian-language destiny matrix readings call “The Emperor” or “The Sovereign”. It is built from cards that are hard to picture side by side: at the entry, the Hanged Man — a man suspended upside down by one foot; as the mechanism, the Tower — a house struck by lightning; at the root, the Emperor on his throne. The tail's scenario is easy to recognise. A person endures and postpones for a long time, even though they see the crack before anyone else — until everything collapses at once, by someone else's will or in their own outburst. Then they build again, and often to the same blueprint. The root card offers a third way between “endure” and “destroy”: to rule — to decide before the lightning strikes. And at the centre of the chart, everyone with this tail has Justice.

sections.h2: Why 12-16-4 is called “The Emperor” and “The Sovereign”
paragraphs: Both names come with the same legend. In a past life, the story goes, this person held power — ruled, commanded an army, led a community — and used it harshly: kept order with an iron hand, counted no cost in lives, may even have been a tyrant. Now the soul is supposedly learning the opposite: to trust, to listen to others, to govern out of love rather than fear, to make peace with the father and to stop controlling everything.

The legend cannot be checked. Numbers say nothing about past lives, and the tarot books on which the meanings of the arcana rest know nothing of the matrix or of karmic tails. But the name “The Emperor” was not plucked from thin air. Open the divinatory lists of Arthur Edward Waite — the author of the classic tarot deck and of the book that serves as its key — and it turns out that all three cards of the tail speak the language of the state.

The Emperor's list holds no surprises: “Stability, power, protection, realization; a great person; aid, reason, conviction; also authority and will.” The surprise lies in the other two cards. Waite describes the Tower reversed with the words “oppression, imprisonment, tyranny”. His Hanged Man reversed reads: “Selfishness, the crowd, body politic.” The body politic is an old English expression for the state understood as a single body in which every subject has a place. Together they make up the full cast of a political drama: subjects and the crowd, tyranny and prison, a sovereign on the throne.

There are no reversed cards in the destiny matrix: a calculated number cannot land upside down. So both of Waite's lists — for the upright and for the reversed position — are read here as two sides of one card, not as a “plus” and a “minus”.

The second clue is the history of the images. In the cities of Renaissance Italy, traitors who had escaped punishment were “executed” on walls: they were painted on the façades of public buildings hanging upside down by one foot, for the whole city to see. These shame paintings, pitture infamanti, were commissioned by the cities' rulers, and some survive as preparatory drawings by Andrea del Sarto — men hanging by the ankle. Tarot historians see in them the prototype of the card. In the fifteenth century it was called both “the Hanged Man” and “the Traitor”, il Traditore. **The first card of the tail depicted the one whom power had hanged.**

The Tower is tied to power as well. Listing its old titles — “Castle of Plutus, God's House and the Tower of Babel” (the Marseille deck labels it La Maison Dieu, the House of God) — Waite adds: “In the last case, the figures falling therefrom are held to be Nimrod and his minister.” In the Book of Genesis, Nimrod is the one who “began to be a mighty one in the earth”, and “the beginning of his kingdom was Babel”. Josephus, in the Antiquities of the Jews, writes of him in words that read like a ready-made description of this tail. Nimrod “gradually changed the government into tyranny, seeing no other way of turning men from the fear of God, but to bring them into a constant dependence on his power” — and promised to build a tower “too high for the waters to be able to reach”. The multitude, Josephus says, “were very ready to follow”. How it ended he tells in the words of the Sibyl: “the gods sent storms of wind and overthrew the tower.”

So the folk name was read correctly from the pictures: 12-16-4 is a tail about power. Where the legend goes wrong is in where it puts the tyrant. In the cards, tyranny stands not at the root but in the middle: it is the Tower, the thing that falls. The Hanged Man is the one hanging under someone else's power. And the Emperor at the root is not a sin from a past life but the task of this one: power that needs no tower. Curiously, the tail's popular “lessons” — learn to trust, govern out of love — repeat almost word for word Waite's second list for the Emperor: “Benevolence, compassion, credit.” In Waite's English, credit means trust and good standing as well as money lent.

sections.h2: The Hanged Man at the entry: a life in suspension
paragraphs: The first card of the tail stands at point M, where the scenario begins. It is the first reaction at the moment a situation becomes truly personal. For 12-16-4 that reaction is to suspend. Not to argue, not to leave, not to decide: to wait, to sit it out, to see which way things turn. To put off the conversation until a better moment. To take on a little more. To hand the decision over to circumstances, to the boss, to the partner, to time.

Point M has a feature that is easy to miss. It opens two routes at once: the karmic tail M → N → D and the relationship line M → R1 → R. So for everyone with 12-16-4, the Hanged Man also stands at the start of the relationship line, and in the chakra table it sits in the energy of Svadhisthana, the chakra of joy and creativity. The suspended state switches on most easily where a person cares most: in intimacy and in the work they love.

The card is called the Hanged Man, but what Waite describes is closer to a man suspended. The tree he hangs from is living wood, with leaves on it. The face “expresses deep entrancement, not suffering”. The figure as a whole, Waite writes, **“suggests life in suspension, but life and not death”**. He rejects the readings through martyrdom, prudence and duty: one “may exhaust all published interpretations and find only vanity”.

Yet the Hanged Man's divinatory list holds a surprising amount of sight: “Wisdom, circumspection, discernment, trials, sacrifice, intuition, divination, prophecy.” This man is not blind. He sees more than others — and hangs.

Benebell Wen, author of the modern textbook Holistic Tarot, adds two details that are decisive for this tail. The first: “The hanged man knew what was going to happen to him before it happened.” The second: the card has another reading, “the unsettling calm before a storm”. In the ordinary deck Death follows the Hanged Man, and Wen speaks of the storm before Death. In the 12-16-4 tail the calm is followed by a different storm: the Tower.

The third detail is the legs. The tau cross they form, in Wen's words, “indicates the balance between dominion and slavery”. In the Marseille deck the crossbar is especially clear: the free leg is tucked behind the other so that it makes an upside-down figure 4. Readers of the cards noticed long ago that the Emperor, the fourth card, crosses his legs the same way — only he sits on a throne. **The Hanged Man is the Emperor upside down**: the same figure of power, only suspended. The tail begins with an inverted sovereign and ends with a sovereign on the throne.

Éliphas Lévi, the French occultist Waite often cites, saw in this card “the adept bound by his engagements”. Waite called the reading shallow, if plausible. For the tail it is more accurate than for the card in general: the bearer of 12-16-4 hangs not from a rope but from promises — made to others, to themselves, to their parents — and from rules accepted long ago.

That is what the entry looks like. A person sees a crack in the house: the job stopped being theirs long ago, the relationship runs on habit, the rule is out of date, the boss is steering the business towards a crash. They see it before others do. And they suspend the situation — along with themselves. Not out of weakness: out of caution, out of loyalty to their word, out of hope of waiting it out.

sections.h2: The Tower as the mechanism: lightning that is waited for
paragraphs: The second card stands at point N, the mechanism that keeps the pattern repeating even when the person already understands everything about themselves. Here stands the Tower, the heaviest card in the deck by its plain meaning. Waite lists: “Misery, distress, indigence, adversity, calamity, disgrace, deception, ruin.” And adds the key point: “It is a card in particular of unforeseen catastrophe.”

But for Waite destruction is only the surface. He agrees with the reading of the Tower as “the ruin of the House of Life, when evil has prevailed therein, and above all … the rending of a House of Doctrine”, and specifies: “the reference is, however, to a House of Falsehood.” He explains the two falling figures this way: “The one is the literal word made void and the other its false interpretation.” And he sets beside them a line from the Psalms: **“except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it.”** The Tower does not bring down just any house, but one built on someone else's foundation or on a false one.

In the deepest sense, Waite writes, the Tower “may signify also the end of a dispensation”. This theological word goes back to the Latin dispensatio, which rendered the Greek oikonomia, literally “the management of a house”; Russian theology renders it as domostroitelstvo, “house-building”. Even here the Tower speaks of a house and of the one who runs it.

Wen describes the same thing from the side of the one who lives through it: “a sudden change, a jolting event that will shake the Seeker to his or her foundation”. But she adds two refinements. “The aftermath is truth.” And: “The old must be destroyed so that the new can be built, this time correctly and for the right reasons.” She compares the Tower directly with Judgement: both cards lead to an epiphany, but Judgement leads on to divine fulfilment, the Tower to rebuilding. For a tail with a builder at its root, the difference matters.

In the 12-16-4 tail the Tower works as a release. The Hanged Man's calm is not empty: everything unsaid and undecided builds up inside it. Sooner or later the tension finds its way out in a single blow, and the blow comes from two sides. From outside — when something the person has long seen cracking gives way: the company closes, the partner leaves, a deception comes to light. From inside — when the one who endured for years breaks everything in a single evening: resigns with one email, packs a suitcase, ends a relationship without explanation. Those around them call it a bolt from the blue. To them the sky was never clear.

Here lies the tail's main paradox. Waite calls the Tower a card “of unforeseen catastrophe”, yet for the bearer of 12-16-4 it is almost always foreseen. The Hanged Man, with his discernment and prophecy, sees the crack years before the collapse, and afterwards says: “I knew it.” **Knew — and waited.**

The mechanism holds because the collapse works. It settles in a day what years of waiting could not, and shows what everything was standing on. The relief can be enormous. That is how the lesson the tail keeps repeating takes hold: **change only comes through catastrophe**. Next time the person suspends the situation again and waits for lightning again — their own or someone else's. And on the ruins they hurry to build something new, often to the old blueprint: under someone else's power again, on promises again, with a crack they can see from day one.

The mechanism also has a political pattern, which Waite built into the Tower reversed: “oppression, imprisonment, tyranny”. The tyranny need not be someone else's. More often it is an order the person submitted to on their own: “one just has to put up with it”, “that's how it's done”, “good children don't argue”, “leaving means betraying”. Nimrod's tower was built to keep people dependent on power. The tower of this tail is a house built on someone else's doctrine — the very House of Falsehood from Waite's book. That is exactly where the lightning strikes.

sections.h2: The Emperor at the root: power that needs no tower
paragraphs: The third card stands at point D, the root to which the whole sequence returns. Here stands the Emperor. Waite describes him as “executive and realization, the power of this world”. His seat, in Waite's words, is “the intellectual throne”: “the lordship of thought rather than of the animal world”. And he notes at once that such power is not yet “the wisdom which draws from a higher world”.

Wen puts the core briefly: “All is in order, under control.” Her Emperor is authority, government, order, jurisdiction, an iron will. But she also sees the price. Behind the Emperor on the Waite–Smith card lie dry, jagged rocks; “the kingdom is parched”, and this is “a thirst for a different kind of sovereignty than the one the Seeker has attained”. Wen recalls King Midas: everything he touched turned to gold, and he died of hunger, because “gold cannot nourish”.

For the tail, the root means one thing: becoming the authority in one's own life. Put the two divinatory lists side by side and the difference is plain. The Hanged Man has wisdom, discernment, prophecy. The Emperor has realization, will, conviction. One sees, the other acts. **The Hanged Man knows the house is cracked; the Emperor rebuilds it.** Between them stands the Tower: it does this work for the person if they do not do it themselves — only it does it with lightning.

The root has a trap, and its outline is in Wen too. Her Emperor reversed means “the overthrow of authority”, a “coup d'état”, “dominating the domineering”. After the Tower, someone who hung for years easily takes the throne vowing “nobody will ever order me around again” — and starts to rule the way they were ruled: everything under control, no pauses, no one else's decisions. The kingdom is parched again, and around the new sovereign others begin to hang. This is how the tyrant of the legend is born — not in a past life but in this one, six months after the collapse.

Waite wrote the way out of the trap into the Emperor's second list: benevolence, compassion, credit — that is, trust. Speaking of a harsh ruler, Wen advises learning “to lead with more compassion and kindness, and less severity”. The root of 12-16-4 is not just any Emperor but a sovereign who remembers what it is like to hang upside down. His power rests not on fear but on stability, protection and trust. Such power needs no tower reaching to the sky: a foundation is enough.

sections.h2: Justice at the centre and the Tower in Manipura
paragraphs: Everyone with the 12-16-4 tail has Justice at the centre of the chart: that is how the arithmetic works, and no other number appears at the centre with this tail. The centre is the comfort zone, the place a person returns to when they feel at ease. Here it is the scales and the sword: a sense that the world ought to be arranged fairly and that effort ought to pay off.

Wen explains Justice in an unexpected way — through Newton's third law: “to every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction”. When a person exerts a particular force, “there will be another force exerted against it, one equal in magnitude and opposite in direction”. For this tail the law reads like a diagram of the mechanism. **Suspension is not the absence of force but force held inside.** The longer it is held, the stronger the recoil. The Tower is a reaction equal to everything that was endured.

Wen draws one more line herself. Justice reversed, for her, is “feeling unjustly wronged”. The Hanged Man reversed, which comes next in her numbering, is martyrdom, and Wen expressly notes the progression from the first to the second. In the 12-16-4 tail this progression is built into the structure of the chart: the centre keeps the account, the entry endures. Beneath the endurance there is often an invisible ledger: “I've put up with so much — I'm owed.” When the scales tip over, the Tower carries out the sentence.

Even in Manipura — the chakra of will, status and money — everyone with 12-16-4 has the same triple: 8-8-16, two Justices and the Tower. Manipura's physics and energy are the centre of the chart, its emotions are their sum, and 8 + 8 makes exactly sixteen. So the Tower appears twice in every such matrix: in the mechanism of the tail and in the emotions of Manipura. One of the Tower's old names in Waite is the “Castle of Plutus”, the god of wealth, and with money the pattern is the same: weighing and saving for a long time — and deciding in one sharp move.

The tail also has an arithmetical beauty. The root is 4, the centre 8, the entry 12, the mechanism 16. All four numbers are multiples of four: the tail together with its centre is the Emperor's times table, and the Tower is his square, 4 × 4. This is a property of the calculation, not a secret meaning, but it is easy to remember: **the whole 12-16-4 loop is built on the number of its root**.

sections.h2: King Lear: the storm that teaches the throne
paragraphs: Shakespeare knew neither the tarot nor the matrix, and the comparison below is ours. But it is hard to find a more exact illustration of the 12-16-4 loop than King Lear: the play begins with scales, passes through suspension and a storm, and ends with the question of what true power is. Quotations follow the original text.

It all begins with Justice in its driest form. The old king divides his kingdom and makes his daughters weigh their love: “Which of you shall we say doth love us most? That we our largest bounty may extend Where nature doth with merit challenge.” The youngest, Cordelia, answers: “Nothing, my lord.” “Nothing will come of nothing,” Lear warns, and she gives him a measure: “I love your majesty According to my bond; no more nor less.” The king hears a zero.

Then the king suspends himself. He wants “To shake all cares and business from our age” and to “Unburden'd crawl toward death”, yet he keeps “The name, and all the addition to a king”, while “the sway, Revenue, execution of the rest” go to his sons-in-law. He no longer rules, but he is still king: he hangs between the throne and the open road and depends on his daughters' goodwill. This is life in suspension, only chosen of his own free will.

Then comes the Tower. Lear goes out into the storm, and the castle gates are shut behind him: “Shut up your doors, my lord; 'tis a wild night.” His speech on the heath sounds like a description of the sixteenth card: “Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks! Rage! blow! … You sulphurous and thought-executing fires, Vaunt-couriers to oak-cleaving thunderbolts, Singe my white head!” And straight after comes the voice of the Hanged Man in Wen's version, the one in the right against a mob in the wrong: “I am a man More sinn'd against than sinning.”

And then comes what makes the play worth rereading. In the storm the king sees his kingdom from below for the first time: “Poor naked wretches, wheresoe'er you are, That bide the pelting of this pitiless storm, How shall your houseless heads and unfed sides … defend you From seasons such as these? O, I have ta'en Too little care of this! Take physic, pomp; Expose thyself to feel what wretches feel, That thou mayst shake the superflux to them And show the heavens more just.” On the ruins of his power Lear finds what it lacked — Waite's second list for the Emperor: compassion and benevolence. And he finds them through Justice: the speech ends with the words “show the heavens more just”.

In the fourth act the mad king, crowned with weeds, explains to the blinded Gloucester how power works: “There thou mightst behold the great image of authority: a dog's obeyed in office.” And he says a line worthy of the Hanged Man: **“change places; and, handy-dandy, which is the justice, which is the thief?”** The judge here is called “the justice” — the same word as the card. The upside-down view turns the scales over. In the same scene, in rags and a crown of weeds, Lear says of himself: “Ay, every inch a king.”

Lear goes through the whole loop, and too late: his reconciliation with Cordelia lasts a single scene, and the ending is tragic. That is why the play works not as a prophecy but as a warning. Everything the king understood in the storm — that power rests on protection, not on weighing love, and that one has to look from below as well — the root of the 12-16-4 tail invites a person to understand on the throne, before the lightning strikes.

sections.h2: How the 12-16-4 loop plays out in life
paragraphs: The scenario is recognised not by its events but by its course: a long pause in which the person sees everything and endures, then a collapse, then hasty building — and a new pause. The scenery changes; the course stays the same.

paragraphs.h3: In a couple: a long silence and a suitcase by the door

paragraphs: A person with this tail rarely makes scenes. They adapt, give way, put off the difficult conversation until better times and live for years with what does not suit them — while seeing the relationship more clearly than their partner does. The partner thinks everything is fine. Then one day comes the final “I'm leaving”, or a packed suitcase stands by the door. For one of them it is a bolt from the blue; for the other, a decision that has been ripening for five years.

There is a mirror version too. The bearer of the tail hangs on, waiting for the other person to change — grow up, get divorced, stop disappearing — and the collapse comes from outside: the other person leaves first. The outcome is the same. The change happened not by decision but by lightning.

paragraphs.h3: At work: the indispensable one who leaves in a day

paragraphs: At work 12-16-4 often looks like the most patient employee in the building. They take on extra, wait for the promised promotion, see that management is steering the business the wrong way, and say nothing — out of caution, out of loyalty, out of hope. They are the first to notice the cracks in the project, in the budget, in the boss. And then either the company collapses exactly where they predicted, or they leave with a single email, and colleagues learn of their discontent on the day they quit.

There is also the reverse role. Once they finally get power — a department, their own business, a crew — the former long-sufferer sometimes rules more harshly than anyone: no one decides for them, no surprises, everything under control. This is the Emperor from Wen's trap: a parched kingdom where others now hang.

paragraphs.h3: In the family: a house where someone ruled

paragraphs: Popular readings advise people with 12-16-4 to “work through accepting the father”, and there is a logic in the card for it: the Emperor is a figure of parental authority. Not necessarily the father — whoever ruled the house: a mother, a grandmother, a stepfather. The scenario often begins in childhood. The child lives by that house's rules for a long time, puts their own wishes off until later, and then breaks free of its power in an explosion: slams the door at seventeen, moves to another city, does not call for years.

The explosion sets them free but does not teach them to rule. So one of two things often follows: either the person again finds a house with a master, or builds their own — with the same rigid rules they ran from. To “accept the father”, in the language of this tail, means to see in parental authority neither a throne nor a prison but people who ruled as best they could, and to take from their house what holds, not what crushes.

The quietest form is internal. For years a person lives with the clear knowledge that things cannot go on like this — and with an equally clear decision to change nothing for now. They brace for the worst, wait for the right moment, estimate when everything will collapse on its own, and in their mind they have already lived through the collapse a dozen times. Wen compares the feeling of suspension to the question the Fool poses: “will the Seeker fall or fly?” The 12-16-4 tail has its own answer: wait until the lightning decides.

paragraphs.h3: With money: years on the scales, a day of lightning

paragraphs: In money and status, where everyone with the tail has Manipura 8-8-16, the pattern is the same. Long, careful calculation, savings for a rainy day, purchases and plans put off — and decisions made in a single day: sell, put everything in, drop it all and start again. The tail predicts neither ruin nor windfalls. It describes a rhythm.

sections.h2: The price: what the tail takes if no one notices it
paragraphs: The first price is a postponed life. A pause meant to last until a better moment stretches into years. Waite's Hanged Man is alive — “life and not death” — but a suspended life stays suspended: the best of one's strength goes into waiting.

The second is a chain of collapses. Each Tower takes what was built over years: relationships, a position, money, a circle of friends. If after each blow one builds to the old blueprint, the collapses repeat, and life turns into a series of fresh starts from zero.

The third is a reputation for suddenness. Others see someone calm, patient, reliable — and then a slammed door. There were warnings, but they sounded on the inside. It is hard for those close to trust someone who leaves without signals, even if that person had been signalling to themselves for years.

The fourth is hardening. Someone who escaped another's power by explosion risks becoming the same kind of power. Waite put “oppression, imprisonment, tyranny” into the Tower reversed, and that tyranny may turn out to be one's own: tight control over the home, the children, subordinates — and oneself.

The fifth is emptiness among the ruins. The Tower, in Wen's words, shakes a person “to his or her foundation”, and afterwards there can be a great void. If a collapse has left despair, if thoughts turn towards self-harm, that is a reason to reach out to a psychologist or psychotherapist straight away, and in danger to call your local emergency number or a local crisis line. A reading of the tail is a language for observing oneself, not a substitute for help.

sections.h2: How to leave the loop: reform instead of revolution
paragraphs: The tail cannot be cancelled, and no “bad card” can be pulled out of it: the Hanged Man, the Tower and the Emperor are resources in themselves. The tail knows two modes — endure and destroy. The root asks for a third — rule. In the language of the state this is called reform instead of revolution: changing the order by decision, in parts and in good time, rather than waiting for it to be swept away.

ol: **Give every pause a deadline.** When putting off a decision, name a date at once: “I'll wait until the first of March, then decide.” A pause with a deadline is circumspection. A pause without one is suspension.

**Write the cracks down.** The Hanged Man sees before anyone else — let that sight work for the person. Once a month, answer on paper: what in life is held together by a promise, and what is being done about it right now. A prophecy with at least one step becomes a plan.

**A small “no” instead of a big explosion.** Voice discontent at the first “I don't want to”, not the hundredth. One awkward sentence on a Monday costs less than a suitcase by the door three years later.

**Check the blueprint before building.** When starting a job, a relationship, a big project, ask: whose house is this? Am I building it because I want to, or because that's how it's done? The psalm Waite quotes says the same in the language of faith: a house built on the wrong foundation is built in vain.

**After a collapse, take time for the truth.** Do not build on the ruins the next day. Wen says that “the aftermath is truth”, and there has to be time to see it: what the false foundation was, which rule fell along with the house.

**Rule without scorched earth.** Having gained power — at home, at work, over oneself — leave room for other people's decisions and for one's own pauses. The sign of the Emperor in the trap: everything under control, and nothing grows.

**Keep the account out loud.** Instead of a secret ledger of “I endure, so I'm owed”, name directly what is missing and what needs agreeing. Justice at the centre works better as an agreement than as a sentence.

**Give way by decision, not by suspension.** Waiting, giving way and sacrificing are all possible — if it is a choice made with open eyes and with a deadline. On the Waite–Smith card the Hanged Man has a nimbus around his head: his sacrifice is conscious, not forced.

paragraphs: The sign that the loop has weakened is simple: **change starts to come by decision, not by catastrophe**. The person changes what has cracked on the day they understand it, not on the day it falls.

sections.h2: The strong version of 12-16-4: a sovereign who remembers hanging upside down
paragraphs: The strong version of the tail is a person who sees earlier than others and acts in time. Their sight comes from the Hanged Man: discernment, circumspection, the ability to look at the familiar from the other side. Their calm in a crisis comes from the Tower: they know what a collapse looks like from inside, keep their head when someone else's house is falling, and understand that after the jolt the truth comes out. Their footing comes from the Emperor: stability, protection, realization.

Such people do well where others wait for lightning: in crisis management, in reform, in construction and restoration, in rescue work, in a family that has to be gathered together after a disaster. People come to them when someone needs to say out loud what everyone sees and stays silent about, and then to take the change on themselves. They know how to build “this time correctly and for the right reasons” — Wen's description of the work after the Tower.

And above all, their power does not turn into a tower. An Emperor who once hung upside down knows what it is like to be below, and rules with what Waite put in the card's second list: benevolence, compassion, trust. Lear understood this in the storm. The strong version of 12-16-4 understands it on the throne, while the sky is still clear.

sections.h2: How to check for the 12-16-4 tail by date of birth
paragraphs: The 12-16-4 tail appears when the three numbers of a birth date add up to 31 or 40: both sums reduce to 4. Here is how to count:

ol: A is the day of birth. If it is greater than 22, add its digits: 29 → 11, 31 → 4.
B is the number of the month.
C is the sum of the digits of the year; if it is greater than 22, add the digits again: 1997 → 26 → 8.
If A + B + C = 31 or 40, the tail is 12-16-4.

paragraphs: Example: 14.07.1990. A = 14, B = 7, C = 1 + 9 + 9 + 0 = 19, sum 40. Everything else falls into place by itself:
A sum of 31 gives the same result: 31 → 4, and the centre is 31 + 4 = 35 → 8. Of all dates with this tail, almost two thirds come from the sum 31 and the rest from the sum 40.

There is also a third route, the shortest: a sum of exactly 4. It is only possible with A = 1, B = 1 and C = 2, which means a single date: 1 January 2000. That is the very day the world awaited with bated breath. The “Year 2000 problem” promised that at midnight computers would confuse 2000 with 1900 and a digital collapse would follow. By estimates, about $300 billion went into preparing for it; the night passed almost quietly, and people still argue over whether the work saved the world or the threat was overblown. The coincidence proves nothing, but for the 12-16-4 tail it is almost a parable: a long wait for the blow, a Tower everyone expects, and the quiet work of order instead of lightning.
From this arithmetic follow facts that are the same for everyone with 12-16-4:

ul: the centre of the chart is always Justice, and Manipura is 8-8-16;
the relationship line always starts with the Hanged Man, and 12 also stands in the energy of Svadhisthana;

the tail is possible on any day of the month and in any year since 1900: even the “poorest” year has at least seven such dates, and years with the year number 19 — 1909, 1918 and so on up to 1990 — have 35 each;
for those born in 1901, 1910, 2009 and 2018, the relationship line repeats the tail in full: 12-16-4.

paragraphs: How many such people are there? We went through every date from 1 January 1900 to 5 October 2026 — 46,299 days. The 12-16-4 tail comes up on 3,115 of them, 6.73%: sixth place out of 26 possible tails, roughly one person in fifteen. But the share falls from generation to generation. It peaks among those born in the 1930s, at 8.6%. Among people born in 1960–1999 it is 6.6%, and in 2000–2025 just 3.7%: children have this tail almost half as often as their parents.

sections.h2: What this reading is based on

ul: The calculation follows the classic destiny matrix scheme: the tail is written as M–N–D, where D = A + B + C, the centre E = A + B + C + D, M = D + E, N = D + M, and sums greater than 22 are reduced by adding their digits. Manipura in the chakra table is E, E and their reduced sum. Frequencies were obtained by running every date through the site's calculator.
Arthur Edward Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910; 1922 reissue): card symbolism — Part II, divinatory meanings — Part III, old titles and variant designs — Part I.
Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015), chapter 9: the Hanged Man, the Tower, the Emperor, Justice.
Flavius Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, Book I, chapter 4, in William Whiston's translation; Genesis 10:8–10; Psalm 127:1 (126:1 in the Septuagint and in Russian Bibles).
The history of the Hanged Man card and of Italian shame paintings — from publicly available surveys of tarot history.
William Shakespeare, King Lear, Acts I, III and IV.
The Year 2000 problem — from publicly available surveys.
The link between the three positions, the comparison with King Lear and the practices are the author's interpretation. Waite and Wen do not describe the destiny matrix or karmic tails.

paragraphs: For a couple, 12-16-4 raises the question of how authority is shared. Here the Hanged Man is the entry to the task, the Tower is its middle, and the Emperor is the main task: rules that leave room for both.

faq.q: Is it true that the 12-16-4 tail goes to someone who was a tyrant in a past life?
faq.a: There are no grounds to think so. The legend of a ruler who governed cruelly in a past incarnation cannot be checked: numbers say nothing about past lives. Its only support is in the images. In Waite's divinatory lists the three cards of the tail speak the language of power, and among the Tower's old titles is the Tower of Babel, from which Nimrod falls. But tyranny in these cards stands in the middle, in the Tower — as the thing that falls. **The Emperor at the root is a task, not a sentence.**

faq.q: Does the Tower in the tail mean disasters, ruin or losing one's home?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events: no bankruptcies, no divorces, no accidents. The Tower as the mechanism describes the way change most often happens in a person's life — sharply and all at once after a long pause. For one person it is a loud exit from a job, for another an inner turning point that nobody noticed. **The calculation describes a possible scenario; it does not assign a fate.**

faq.q: Why do I also have the Tower in Manipura?
faq.a: Because everyone with 12-16-4 has 8 at the centre of the chart, and Manipura is calculated from the centre: physics 8, energy 8, emotions 8 + 8 = 16. So their Manipura triple is always 8-8-16, and the Tower appears in the matrix twice. This is not a doubling of misfortune but the same pattern in another theme: in will, status and money, too, decisions are weighed for a long time and then made abruptly.

faq.q: Are the 12-16-4 tail and “4-16-12” the same thing?
faq.a: No. In a karmic tail the order is set by the formula: M is the entry, N the mechanism, D the root, and the numbers cannot be rearranged. The calculator never produces 4-16-12 in the tail position; under that spelling, searches turn up both this tail written backwards and combinations from other parts of the chart. If it is the tail that is meant, its root is always 4, the Emperor, and its entry is always 12, the Hanged Man.

faq.q: Why is the 12-16-4 tail rarer among children than among their parents?
faq.a: Because of the year number. For this tail to appear, the day, the month and the year number must add up to 31 or 40. In the twentieth century, four years out of five had a year number between 10 and 22, and such sums came easily. After 2000 the year number became small, from 2 to 12, and the day and month have to make up almost everything themselves. So among people born in 1960–1999, 6.6% have the 12-16-4 tail, and among those born in 2000–2025, 3.7%. This is calendar arithmetic, not a sign of a generation's special fate.

faq.q: Why do I have 12-16-4 both in the karmic tail and in the relationship line?
faq.a: Both lines start at the same point M, so the Hanged Man stands at the start of the relationship line for everyone with this tail. A full match happens when the year number is 11: since 1900 these are the years 1901, 1910, 2009 and 2018. This holds for 88 of the 3,115 dates with this tail, about one in 35. Then one and the same scenario describes both the karmic loop and the way of building a couple, and relationships are where it is most useful to watch it.

It shares the Hanged Man at the entry with 12-19-7, but after that the paths diverge: there the mechanism is the Sun and the root is the Chariot, the card of movement and victory. In 12-16-4 the pause is released through collapse, and the root asks not for movement but for structure — a throne and order. With 21-10-16 it shares the Tower, but there the Tower stands at the root, as the task itself, while here it works as the mechanism — a blow that repeats while the person waits.

There is no ritual that cancels a tail, and the numbers of a date do not change. What changes is something else: the scenario stops switching on automatically. The signs are that pauses get deadlines, discontent is voiced early and calmly, after a hard period the person does not build something new the very next day, and change in their life comes by decision rather than by lightning.

faq.q: What if a child has the 12-16-4 tail?
faq.a: Better not to retell the legend of the past-life tyrant to the child: a label easily becomes a programme. It helps more to teach them to say “I don't want to” in good time and not to punish them for it. If a child endures for a long time and then explodes, look for the start in the pause, not in the outburst: notice when they silently put up with something uncomfortable, and ask before it comes to an explosion. And give them a little real power — their own shelf, their own decisions about free time, the right to change the rules in their own room.

faq.q: Is the 12-16-4 tail different for women and men?
faq.a: No. Sex plays no part in the calculation and does not change the numbers, so the tail and its scenario are the same. The Emperor at the root is not a male role or a duty to be head of the family, but the ability to run one's own life. Only the scenery differs: whose power presses down, where the person endures longest and where the collapse comes.

faq.q: Why is 8 Justice here, when tarot books make 8 Strength?
faq.a: The destiny matrix counts by the old Marseille numbering: 8 is Justice, 11 is Strength. Waite swapped these two cards in his deck and explains it himself in the chapter on Strength, so in books based on his deck Justice is numbered XI. The meaning of the card does not depend on the number: it is carried by the name and the image — the scales and the sword.

intro: The cards here are numbered as in the destiny matrix and in the Marseille deck: 8 is Justice. In Waite's deck this card is numbered XI, but its meaning rests on its name and image, not on the number.

head: Position
Arcanum
Role in the scenario
rows: the first reaction is to suspend: put off the decision, sit it out, hand one's will over to circumstances or to someone else
release through collapse: what was put off for years is settled in a single blow
authority over one's own life: deciding and building before the lightning strikes
shared by everyone with this tail: scales, order, an inner ledger of what is “fair”

report: The catastrophe that everyone around calls a bolt from the blue was usually visible to the person with the 12-16-4 tail years before it struck. They saw the job crack, and the relationship, and the rule they lived by. And they waited. Then everything collapses at once — from outside or in their own outburst — and out comes the inevitable: “I knew it.”

Popular readings call this tail “The Emperor” and explain the name with a legend: in a past life the person was supposedly a ruler, perhaps a tyrant, and is now learning trust and how to govern out of love. The legend cannot be checked: numbers say nothing about past lives. But the name does not rest on the legend alone. All three cards of the tail speak the language of the state. In Waite's divinatory lists the Emperor has “Stability, power, protection, realization”, the Tower “oppression, imprisonment, tyranny”, and the Hanged Man “the crowd” and the body politic, the state seen as a single body.

The images have a history too. In the cities of Renaissance Italy, traitors who had fled were “executed” on walls: rulers commissioned shame paintings in which the fugitive hung upside down by one foot. In the fifteenth century the Hanged Man card was also called “the Traitor”. And from the Tower, in one of the old readings Waite cites, falls Nimrod — the man who, in Josephus's words, “gradually changed the government into tyranny” to keep people in a constant dependence on his power. **The first card of the tail shows the one whom power hanged; the second, the fall of a tyrant.** In the cards, tyranny stands not at the root but in the middle: it is the thing that falls.

report.h3: He sees more than anyone — and hangs

report: The Hanged Man at the entry is the first reaction when a matter turns personal: suspend it. Put off the conversation, sit it out, take on a little more, hand the decision over to circumstances. Waite rejects reading this card through martyrdom: the tree is living wood, the face “expresses deep entrancement, not suffering”, and the whole figure **“suggests life in suspension, but life and not death”**. The card's divinatory list holds a surprising amount of sight: wisdom, discernment, intuition, prophecy. Benebell Wen adds: “The hanged man knew what was going to happen to him before it happened” — and sees in the card “the unsettling calm before a storm”.

What holds the person is not rope but promises and rules: “one just has to put up with it”, “that's how it's done”, “leaving means betraying”. In the Marseille deck the Hanged Man's legs cross in an upside-down figure 4 — just like the Emperor's on his throne. The Hanged Man is the Emperor upside down.

The Tower as the mechanism works as a release. In the calm, everything unsaid and undecided builds up, and one day it comes out in a single blow: something long cracked gives way, or the patient one breaks everything in a single evening — resigns with one email, packs a suitcase. Waite calls the Tower a card “of unforeseen catastrophe”. The paradox of the tail is that for its bearer the catastrophe is almost always foreseen.

And it is not just any house that falls. Waite sees in the Tower “the rending of a House of Doctrine”, a House of Falsehood, and sets beside it a line from the Psalms: **“except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it.”** The lightning strikes a house built on someone else's doctrine.

The mechanism holds because the collapse works. In a day it settles what years of waiting could not, and it brings relief. So the lesson takes hold: **change only comes through catastrophe**. On the ruins the person hurries to build anew to the old blueprint — and waits for lightning again.

At the centre of the chart everyone with this tail has Justice. Wen explains it through Newton's third law: “to every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction”. Suspension is not the absence of force but force held inside, and the longer it is held, the stronger the recoil. Beneath the endurance there is often an invisible ledger: “I've put up with so much — I'm owed.” When the scales tip over, the Tower carries out the sentence.

report.h3: The tyrant is born six months after the collapse

report: The Emperor at the root is a task: to become the authority in one's own life. The Hanged Man has wisdom and prophecy; the Emperor has realization, will, conviction. One sees, the other acts. The Tower does this work for the person if they do not do it themselves — only it does it with lightning.

But the root has a trap. Someone who escaped another's power by explosion easily takes the throne vowing “nobody will ever order me around again”, and rules the way they were ruled: everything under control, no pauses, no one else's decisions. Wen writes of the Emperor's parched kingdom and recalls Midas, who died of hunger because “gold cannot nourish”. This is how the tyrant of the legend is born — not in a past life but in this one.

Waite wrote the way out into the Emperor's second list: benevolence, compassion, credit — that is, trust. The tail's popular “lessons” repeat it almost word for word. Shakespeare's Lear reaches the same place only in the storm, after seeing his kingdom from below: “change places; and, handy-dandy, which is the justice, which is the thief?”
The tail knows two modes — endure and destroy. The root asks for a third — rule: change the order by decision, in parts and in good time.

ul: give every pause a deadline: “I'll wait until the first of March, then decide”;
write down the cracks that show up before anyone else sees them, and add at least one step to each;
voice discontent at the first “I don't want to”, not the hundredth;
before building, ask whose house it is and whose blueprint;
after a collapse, do not build the next day; first make out what the false foundation was;
once in power, leave room for other people's decisions.

report: If a collapse has left despair and thoughts of self-harm, that is a reason to reach out to a psychologist or psychotherapist straight away, and in danger to call a local emergency number or crisis line.

The strong version of 12-16-4 sees earlier than others and acts in time. It stays calm in a crisis because it knows collapse from the inside, and it can build, in Wen's words, “this time correctly and for the right reasons”. **It is a sovereign who remembers what it is like to hang upside down** — and who rules while the sky is still clear.
